deep.reconstruction:
The page is a table of biquadratic (quartic) characters of four small integers q = -7, +5, -3, +3. Each is taken with respect to every rational prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) below 200, given as a Gaussian prime factor.

The moduli. There are 21 such primes: 5, 13, 17, 29, 37, 41, 53, 61, 73, 89, 97, 101, 109, 113, 137, 149, 157, 173, 181, 193, 197. Each is written as p = N(π) with π = a+bi, a ≡ 1 (mod 4) and b even. Examples: 5 = 1+2i, 13 = -3+2i, 53 = -7+2i, 173 = 13+2i, 197 = 1-14i. One of the two conjugates is fixed once and used consistently in all four tables; the norms all check.

What the columns mean (my interpretation, verified numerically). For each q the primes are sorted into four columns A, B, C, D by the value of the quartic residue symbol [q/π] ≡ q^{(p-1)/4} (mod π):
- A: [q/π] = +1, i.e. q is a biquadratic residue.
- B: [q/π] = +i.
- C: [q/π] = -1, i.e. a quadratic residue but not a quartic residue.
- D: [q/π] = -i.
To evaluate i (mod π), use a+bi ≡ 0, so i ≡ -a·b^{-1} (mod p). Example for p = 5, π = 1+2i: i ≡ 2, and -7 ≡ 3 ≡ -i, so 5 is in column D under -7. Example for p = 13, π = -3+2i: i ≡ 8, and (-7)^3 ≡ 8 = i, so 13 is in column B.

Completeness. Under -7 all 21 primes appear (5+6+4+6). Under +5 the prime 5 itself is omitted, leaving 20 (4+7+4+5). Under -3 and +3 all 21 appear (4+7+5+5 and 4+8+5+4).

Visible regularities (my remarks).
- q = 5: column A is exactly {101, 109, 149, 181}, the primes whose even component b is divisible by 5. This is the classical criterion that 5 is a quartic residue mod p = a²+b² iff 5 | b. Columns A∪C are the p ≡ ±1 (mod 5).
- q = -7: A∪C are the primes with p a quadratic residue mod 7. By biquadratic reciprocity [-7/π] = [π/7] ≡ π^{12} (mod 7). For example, π = -7+2i ≡ 2i gives (2i)^{12} = 2^{12} ≡ 1.
- q = ±3: A∪C are the primes p ≡ 1 (mod 12). The two tables are linked by [-3/π] = [-1/π][3/π], with [-1/π] = (-1)^{(p-1)/4}. Checked for every prime: entries are identical for p ≡ 1 (mod 8), and A↔C, B↔D are swapped for p ≡ 5 (mod 8).

Purpose. This is empirical material for Gauss's theory of biquadratic residues: finding criteria for the quartic character of small primes in terms of a, b, and testing biquadratic reciprocity. It fits the preceding page, which works with Gaussian moduli such as -1+2i and the modulus 3 with residue/index tables.
errors: No errors found. I computed and confirmed a large sample: all of q = ±3 via the [-1/π] consistency check over all 21 primes; for q = 5 the primes 13, 17, 37, 173, 193, 197; for q = -7 the primes 5, 13, 53, 181; for q = -3 the primes 5, 29, 37. All other entries were checked only through the column-union (quadratic character) and counting tests, which they pass. Every prime appears exactly once per table, except 5 under +5, which is correctly excluded.

results.what: Table of the quartic residue character [q/π] ∈ {1, i, -1, -i} for q = -7, 5, -3, 3 and all Gaussian primes π of norm p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 200, with π = a+bi normalized a ≡ 1 mod 4, b even
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (theory of biquadratic residues, 1825/1828 and 1832 memoirs; Nachlass material printed in Werke II)

results.what: Implicit criterion: 5 is a biquadratic residue mod p = a²+b² (b even) iff 5 | b
results.modern_name: Quartic residuacity criterion for 5 (rational quartic reciprocity type)
results.usually_credited_to: Lebesgue/Dirichlet style criteria; Gauss knew such criteria from his biquadratic work

results.what: Implicit use of [-7/π] = [π/7] = π^{12} mod 7 and [-3/π] = [-1/π][3/π]
results.modern_name: Biquadratic reciprocity and multiplicativity of the quartic symbol
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (stated); proofs by Jacobi and Eisenstein (1844)

deep.surprise_reason: These are numerical tables of quartic characters of small primes, the kind of empirical data Gauss is well known to have computed for his biquadratic residue memoirs and Nachlass notes. The only mild point of interest is the normalization a ≡ 1 mod 4 rather than his 1832 'primary' convention, which is irrelevant for rational q.

checkable.asserts: Under -7, p=5 with pi=1+2i: i ≡ -a/b = -1/2 ≡ 2 mod 5, and (-7)^1 ≡ 3 ≡ -i, so 5 is in column D.
Under -7, p=13 with pi=-3+2i: i ≡ 3/2 ≡ 8 and (-7)^3 ≡ 8 = i, so 13 is in column B.
-7 is a biquadratic residue mod 53 (column A under -7).
Under -7, p=181 with pi=9+10i gives [-7/pi] = i (column B).
Column A under +5 is exactly the set of quartic residues of 5.
Under +5, p=193 with pi=-7-12i: i ≡ 7/(-12) mod 193 = 112, and 5^48 ≡ 112, i.e. i (column B).
Under +5, p=173 with pi=13+2i: 5^43 ≡ 13/2 ≡ -i, so 173 is in column D.
Column A under -3 is exactly the set of quartic residues of -3.
Column A under +3 is exactly the set of quartic residues of 3.
Column A under -7 is exactly the set of quartic residues of -7.
All the decompositions p = a²+b² on the page are correct.
The normalization used is a ≡ 1 mod 4 with b even.
